prayer.text: Holy Spirit, protector of the Church, guide us into all truth.

cues.text: A Church Facing the Modern World
Three centuries after Trent, Pope Pius IX confronted a Church challenged on multiple fronts.
Rationalism, materialism, and religious liberalism rose in European intellectual life.
More immediately, Italian nationalist forces steadily dismantled the Papal States , reducing papal temporal territory by the late 1860s to Rome and its immediate surroundings.
Pius IX announced his intention to convoke a general council in 1867 and formally summoned it by the bull Aeterni Patris in June 1869.
The council opened at St. Peter's Basilica on December 8, 1869, drawing some seven hundred bishops from across the Catholic world — the largest assembly of bishops the Church had yet gathered.
Faith and Reason: Dei Filius
The council's first major achievement, the dogmatic constitution Dei Filius , addressed the relationship between faith and reason.

It affirmed that God's existence can be known with certainty through natural reason from the created world, while insisting that revealed truths accessible only through faith do not contradict, but rather complement, sound reasoning.
The constitution explicitly condemned both rationalism, which subordinated revelation entirely to human reason, and fideism, which dismissed reason's competence to support faith at all.
This document represented the council's considered response to currents of nineteenth-century philosophy and science that many bishops saw as eroding traditional religious belief across Europe.
The Definition of Papal Infallibility
The council's best-known and most contested achievement was the constitution Pastor Aeternus , defining the dogma of papal infallibility .
When the pope speaks ex cathedra — formally, as shepherd and teacher of all Christians — he defines a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church.
Through the assistance promised to Peter, he possesses the same infallibility Christ willed his Church to enjoy in matters of doctrine.

The question provoked intense debate before and during the council; a minority of bishops, including many from Germany, France, and the United States, argued the definition was theologically sound but pastorally "inopportune" given the political climate.
On July 18, 1870 , the constitution passed by an overwhelming majority — 433 in favor, 2 opposed, with most dissenting bishops having already left Rome rather than vote against it.
Interrupted by War
The very next day, July 19, 1870 , the Franco-Prussian War broke out, drawing away the French garrison that had protected Rome from the surrounding Kingdom of Italy.
On September 20, 1870 , Italian troops breached the walls of Rome and completed the unification of Italy, ending a millennium of papal temporal sovereignty over the city.
Pius IX, refusing to recognize the seizure, withdrew into the Vatican, declaring himself a "prisoner," and the council was indefinitely suspended without a formal close.

Many planned topics — including a fuller treatment of the Church's own nature and structure — were left unaddressed, an unfinished agenda that would not be taken up again until the Second Vatican Council nearly a century later.
Legacy
Vatican I's definition of papal infallibility remains one of the most consequential dogmatic statements of the modern Catholic Church.
Among some Christians, it remains one of the Church's most controversial, sharpening distinctions between Catholic and other Christian understandings of doctrinal authority.
It also prompted a small but lasting Old Catholic schism among those who rejected the definition.
The council's abrupt, unresolved suspension — rather than a formal close — left it uniquely incomplete among the twenty-one councils.
Its interrupted agenda served as an explicit point of reference for Pope St. John XXIII when he convened the Second Vatican Council in 1962.
